title: HeapShot sampler and latency triage notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note describing a lightweight sampling approach we call 'HeapShot' plus a short triage runbook for intermittent latency regressions that look tied to memory pressure and short-lived CPU hotspots. The goal is pragmatic: produce actionable artifacts (stack snapshots, short-lived heap profiles, a compact trace tarball) that can be attached to perf CI runs or uploaded to an incident ticket so SREs/engineers can form hypotheses quickly.

Why HeapShot?
- Traditional continuous profilers give lots of data but are heavyweight for nightly/PR runs or for short incidents.
- Flamegraphs from perf are great for CPU but miss allocation/heap context and short-lived GC spikes.
- HeapShot attempts to combine three cheap signals: periodic heap allocations (jemalloc/malloc hooks or pprof), eBPF sampled stacks, and allocation-site tagging to correlate CPU + allocation hotspots.

When to use this doc
- Intermittent P50->P99 latency jumps with correlated RSS growth or repeated GC pauses.
- Perf CI indicates a regression in a PR but flamegraphs are inconclusive.
- Memory fragmentation suspected (long upticks in resident set over a short request burst).

HeapShot components and rationale:
1) jemalloc brief snapshot (jemalloc_stats+prof): sample allocator state at short intervals (1s) using MALLOC_CONF or via jemalloc mallctl when available. Provides: active bytes, allocated-by-size-bins, fragmentation estimate. Cheap and informative for heap pressure.

2) eBPF stack sampler (userland + kernel stacks): using simplebpf/usdt sampler that captures sample stacks at ~200Hz for short windows (10s). We keep only ordered call stacks and counts. Advantage: captures CPU stacks that coincide with allocation bursts or lock contention without heavy overhead.

3) pprof heap/alloc samples (process-local): invoke a short heap profile via pprof endpoints where available (internal /debug/pprof/heap?duration=5s) or run the sampling allocator profile API to get allocation site distribution. This ties allocation sites to code paths.

4) contextual metadata: request route, model name, token length distribution, model variant, KV-cache hit ratio, and concurrent connection count. Small JSON metadata attached to every capture.

Typical capture flow (scripted):
- Preconditions: target machine has ptrace/ptrace-scope permissions OR agent running under rpm user; bpftrace and pprof helpers installed.
- Capture window: 10-30s during a reproducible workload (loadgen or synthetic request that reproduces the spike).

Example run (bash, lightweight):

# Collect jemalloc stats periodically and dump to /tmp/heapshot.tar
mkdir -p /tmp/heapshot && cd /tmp/heapshot
# 1) spawn jemalloc stat sampler (requires binary built with jemalloc)
nohup bash -c '
  for i in $(seq 1 10); do
    timestamp=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
    echo "$timestamp" >> jemalloc-samples.txt
    # mallctl can be replaced with exported /debug/jemalloc endpoint when present
    /usr/local/bin/jemallocctl stats >> jemalloc-samples.txt 2>&1
    sleep 1
  done
' &
JEMALLOC_PID=$!

# 2) eBPF sampler (user stacks only, requires bpftrace)
bpftrace -e '
  profile:200hz /comm == "redwood-runtime"/ { @[ustack] = count(); }
  interval:s:10 { exit(); }
' > bpf-stacks.txt 2>/dev/null

# 3) short pprof heap capture (if http pprof endpoint exists)
if curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/heap?seconds=5 -o pprof-heap.pb.gz; then
  echo "pprof captured" >> capture.log
fi

# package artifacts for ticket
tar czf heapshot-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).tgz jemalloc-samples.txt bpf-stacks.txt pprof-heap.pb.gz capture.log metadata.json

Note: the above uses a tiny sampling period to avoid saturating CI. For a deeper capture we extend interval and sampling frequency.

Script catalog (what we keep in repo):
- tools/heapshot/run-heapshot.sh (wrapper that performs the above steps and uploads to S3/CI artifact store)
- tools/heapshot/parse-bpf-stacks.py (collapse stacks into callers|callees counts; output folded stack for flamegraph)
- tools/heapshot/jemalloc-summarize.rb (small script to turn jemalloc text dumps into per-size bucket CSV)
- tools/heapshot/attach-metadata.sh (collects route headers, model variant, concurrency)

Integration with perf CI:
- Strategy: add a HeapShot stage as an optional, low-cost capture step gated by labels on PRs. Only run when tests detect a 10%+ regression in P95 latency or RSS growth above baseline.
- Artifacts: heapshot-YYYYMMDD.tgz uploaded to the PR build artifacts with a link posted to the PR comment.
- Retention: 30 days by default, longer if attached to a release candidate.

Example perf CI job YAML (sketch):
- name: heapshot-capture (conditional)
  if: steps.latency_check.outputs.regressed == 'true'
  run: |
    ./tools/heapshot/run-heapshot.sh --target http://localhost:8080 --duration 20 --out artifacts/heapshot.tgz
  upload-artifact: artifacts/heapshot.tgz

Runbook: quick triage steps when a heapshot artifact is attached
1) Inspect metadata.json: is model variant different? token length higher? concurrency higher? If yes, correlate with changes in PR.
2) Open jemalloc-samples.txt: look for run-away 'active' bytes between snapshots. If active grows steadily across the run without drop, suspect leaking allocations or cache not being reclaimed.
3) Convert bpf-stacks.txt to folded stacks (tools/heapshot/parse-bpf-stacks.py) and render a flamegraph (flamegraph.pl). Look for heavy counts in small set of call stacks — common culprits: KV cache serialization, batch builder, tokenizer, or GC stalling.
4) Inspect pprof-heap.pb.gz (pprof tool) to map allocation-sites; if pprof dominated by one or two functions, correlate with bpf stacks.
5) If collections show many tiny allocations with same callsite, consider switching to object-pool or arena allocation for that structure.
6) If fragmentation high (jemalloc fragmentation metric > 20%), test a repro with madvise/free hints and consider advising the allocator via mallctl tuning.

Common signals and heuristics:
- Rapid RSS growth + low CPU: likely allocations not being freed (background GC not triggered).
- High CPU + modest RSS: compute-bound path; bpf stacks will show hot loops.
- High user+sys CPU + heavy lock contention: look for syscalls in folded stacks (epoll, futex).
- Hot allocation sites but low total bytes: allocation churn (short-lived objects causing GC pressure).

Shareable triage checklist (copy to incident ticket):
- [ ] Include heapshot tarball and metadata.json
- [ ] Confirm service commit running and model version
- [ ] Attach perf CI regression graph (P50/P90/P99)
- [ ] Attach folded flamegraph from bpf stack sampler
- [ ] Attach pprof allocation map (if available)
- [ ] Note whether regression is reproducible locally

Troubleshooting notes (gotchas we've seen):
- bpftrace permission errors: the CI runner must have CAP_BPF or run on a runner image with bpftrace preinstalled. We fall back to perf if bpf not available.
- jemalloc stats format differs by version; the summarizer script normalizes several common formats.
- pprof endpoints may OOM the service if collection is long; keep heap pprof duration short (<= 5s) in CI.
- When collecting on dedicated nodes with GPU, ensure the sampler ignores GPU worker processes to avoid huge binary stacks introduced by vendor libs (NCCL/cuBLAS). We filter by comm name.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should HeapShot be exposed as a long-running agent for staging clusters so we can automatically capture transient events with low overhead? (Pros: capture in prod-like environment; Cons: storage and security).
- Evaluate jemalloc vs tcmalloc snapshot parity on our images (some images use tcmalloc). Need small adapter for tcmalloc stats.
- Add standard label schema for 'heapshot: true' on long-running test jobs so we can find captures easily.

Next steps / TODOs
- [ ] Move run-heapshot.sh into infra/tools and add unit tests for parsing scripts.
- [ ] Add a small GH Action step that posts a summarised output (top-3 stacks, top-3 alloc sites) in PR comments for fast triage.
- [ ] Prototype a lightweight agent that keeps a rolling circular buffer and dumps only around a detected anomaly window.

References and related artifacts:
- Link to internal GC notes: confluence://pages/ENG-allocs (placeholder)
- Existing flamegraph tooling: github.com/redwood-inference/infra-flamegraph (related but complementary)
- Prior incident ENG-3197 notes: slack thread link included in linked_artifacts

Notes to self (scratch):
- If we can attach request-id headers to capture metadata automatically, triage is 10x faster.
- Consider integrating with Optimize to correlate model quantization changes with allocation patterns.

If you take anything away: start small (10s captures) and prioritize metadata. Few short, well-labeled artifacts beat one noisy continuous profiler for incident TTR.
